name: Left ventricle
func: The heart's strongest pumping chamber. It squeezes oxygen-rich blood out through the aortic valve into the aorta, pushing it to every part of the body.

levels.kid:
Your heart has four little rooms. The **left ventricle** is the biggest, strongest room, down at the bottom left. Its walls are thick muscle, like a strong fist.

Blood that just picked up fresh air from your lungs flows into it. Then — squeeze! — it pushes that blood out into a giant tube called the aorta. From there the blood travels all the way to your toes, your fingers and your brain.

It does this about once every second, all day and all night, even while you sleep. It never takes a break. That steady thump you feel in your chest is your left ventricle hard at work.
levels.hs:
The **left ventricle (LV)** is the heart's main pump. It forms the **apex** (the pointed tip, which points down, forward and to the left) and most of the heart's left border and underside. It sits behind the right ventricle, with the **interventricular septum** between them, and below the left atrium.

Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium, then flows through the **mitral valve** into the LV. When the LV contracts (**systole**), the mitral valve snaps shut and the **aortic valve** opens, sending blood into the **aorta** and out to the whole body (the **systemic circulation**).

Because it must push against high pressure, its wall is about **three times thicker** than the right ventricle's (roughly 8–12 mm). Inside, the wall has muscular ridges called **trabeculae carneae** and two **papillary muscles** that anchor the mitral valve's cords.

Each beat ejects about 70 mL of blood. The fraction of blood pumped out per beat is the **ejection fraction**, normally above about 55%.
levels.college:
The LV has a conical cavity that is circular in cross-section, wrapped by a thick myocardial wall, whereas the crescent-shaped right ventricle drapes over the septum. Its inflow (mitral) and outflow (aortic) orifices sit side by side at the base, separated only by the **aortomitral continuity** (fibrous tissue, not muscle), which is why the anterior mitral leaflet forms part of the outflow tract.

The **anterolateral** and **posteromedial papillary muscles** each send **chordae tendineae** to both mitral leaflets. The upper septum near the aortic valve is thin and fibrous (**membranous septum**); the rest is thick and muscular.

The cardiac cycle: during **isovolumetric contraction** all valves are closed and pressure climbs; when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg), the aortic valve opens and **ejection** begins, peaking near 120 mmHg. Then **isovolumetric relaxation**, then filling, which happens in an early passive phase (E wave on echo) and a late phase driven by atrial contraction (A wave).

**Stroke volume** depends on **preload** (stretch at end-diastole), **afterload** (the resistance it pumps against) and **contractility**. The **Frank–Starling law** says a more stretched ventricle contracts more forcefully.

Blood supply: mostly the **LAD** (anterior wall, anterior two-thirds of the septum, apex) and the **circumflex** (lateral wall), with the inferior wall from whichever artery gives the posterior descending artery.
levels.phd:
LV myocardium is organized as a helical continuum: fibers run as a **right-handed helix in the subendocardium**, become circumferential in the mid-wall, and turn into a **left-handed helix in the subepicardium**. This produces **torsion** (wringing) during systole and elastic recoil (untwisting) that creates diastolic suction, a key part of early filling. Speckle-tracking echocardiography measures this as **global longitudinal strain**, which often falls before ejection fraction does.

Cardiomyocytes couple through **intercalated discs** (gap junctions of connexin-43 plus desmosomes). Contraction follows **excitation–contraction coupling**: the action potential opens L-type Ca²⁺ channels in T-tubules, triggering **calcium-induced calcium release** from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via **RyR2**. Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, letting myosin cross-bridges cycle on actin. Relaxation requires active reuptake by **SERCA2a** (regulated by phospholamban), so diastole uses energy too.

The Frank–Starling mechanism works partly through **length-dependent activation**: stretch increases the Ca²⁺ sensitivity of myofilaments, with the giant spring protein **titin** helping set passive stiffness.

Under chronic pressure overload, myocytes add sarcomeres in parallel (**concentric hypertrophy**); under volume overload they add them in series (**eccentric hypertrophy**). **Laplace's law** (wall stress ∝ pressure × radius / wall thickness) explains why: a thicker wall normalizes stress. Pathological remodeling involves fibroblast activation, collagen deposition and a fetal gene program. The subendocardium is the most vulnerable layer to ischemia, because it is compressed during systole and is furthest from the epicardial arteries.
levels.expert:
On exam the LV is felt as the **apex beat**, normally in the **5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line**. A **displaced, diffuse** apex suggests LV dilation; a **heaving, sustained** apex suggests hypertrophy. An **S3** gallop points to a volume-loaded, failing ventricle; an **S4** to a stiff, hypertrophied one.

Key conditions: **heart failure with reduced ejection fraction** (EF under 40%), **heart failure with preserved EF** (stiff ventricle, impaired relaxation), **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** (asymmetric septal thickening with possible outflow obstruction and sudden-death risk in young athletes), **dilated cardiomyopathy**, and **myocardial infarction**. On ECG, **LV hypertrophy** shows tall voltages; an **anterior MI** shows ST elevation in V1–V4 (LAD territory).

Complications after a large MI include **LV aneurysm**, **LV thrombus** (a source of embolic stroke, a direct link to neurosurgery and neurology), **papillary muscle rupture** with acute mitral regurgitation, **ventricular septal rupture** and **free wall rupture**.

Imaging: **echocardiography** is first line (EF, wall motion, valves); **cardiac MRI** with late gadolinium enhancement maps scar and is the reference standard for volumes. **BNP/NT-proBNP** rise with wall stress.

Treatment in general terms: drugs that block the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and sympathetic systems, SGLT2 inhibitors and diuretics for failure; revascularization for ischemia; **implantable defibrillators** for arrhythmia risk; and for end-stage disease, **LV assist devices (LVADs)** or transplantation. LVAD patients need anticoagulation, which matters if they ever need emergency neurosurgery for a bleed.

keyPoints: Forms the apex of the heart, behind the right ventricle
Pumps oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta
Wall about 3× thicker than the right ventricle's
Apex beat: 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
An LV thrombus after MI can cause embolic stroke

test.q: Which valve lets blood INTO the left ventricle?
test.explain: Blood flows from the left atrium through the mitral valve into the LV; it leaves through the aortic valve.

test.q: Why is the LV wall much thicker than the RV wall?
choices: It must generate the high pressure of the systemic circulation
It receives blood from the lungs
test.explain: Systemic pressure (~120 mmHg) is much higher than pulmonary pressure (~25 mmHg), so the LV needs more muscle.

test.q: The percentage of LV blood pumped out with each beat is the ______.
test.explain: Ejection fraction = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume; normally above about 55%.

test.q: A third heart sound (S3) in an adult most suggests:
test.explain: S3 comes from rapid filling into a dilated, volume-loaded ventricle; S4 from atrial contraction into a stiff one.

test.q: The law saying a more stretched ventricle contracts more forcefully is the ______ law.
test.explain: Increased preload stretches sarcomeres and raises myofilament Ca²⁺ sensitivity, increasing stroke volume.
